sig: Warm scones with jam and cream
ds: An old-school English tea room on a quiet lane just off Kensington High Street. People come for the warm toasted scones with jam and Devon cream, and it does a proper full English in the morning too.

a: 332 Bethnal Green Road, Bethnal Green, London E2 0AG
ds: The Pellicci family has run this East End café since 1900. The tiny room is Grade II listed, with Art Deco wood panels, and the welcome is as famous as the big fry-ups and homemade Italian dishes.
A 1946 London caff with a black-tiled Art Deco front, Formica tables and boxing photos on the walls. You order at the counter. You may know the room from films like Layer Cake and Pride.

n: Fortnum & Mason Diamond Jubilee Tea Salon
a: 4th Floor, Fortnum & Mason, 181 Piccadilly, London W1A 1ER
ds: Fortnum & Mason has sold tea on Piccadilly since 1707. Its tea salon was opened by Queen Elizabeth II in 2012, and it is one of the most famous places in London for a full afternoon tea.

a: 87 Tower Bridge Road, Bermondsey, London SE1 4TW
ds: Often called London's oldest surviving pie and mash shop. The green-tiled room is Grade II listed, and the Manze family still runs it, now into the fourth generation.
A Roman Road Market favourite from the Kelly pie and mash family, which started in Bethnal Green in 1915. Expect marble tables, Art Deco fittings and pies with buttery pastry.
The Cooke family has made pie and mash since 1862, and the recipe is said to be unchanged. It is liquor only here, never gravy, served at marble-topped tables.

a: 22 King William Walk, Greenwich, London SE10 9HU
ds: A family pie and mash business since 1890, on a cobbled street facing the National Maritime Museum. The big dining hall has classic bench seats for over 100 people.
The first Poppies, started by East End fryer Pat 'Pop' Newland, who began in the trade aged 11. A retro diner with British fish delivered daily and chips cooked twice.

a: 47 Endell Street, Covent Garden, London WC2H 9AJ
sig: Cod, haddock or plaice and chips
ds: Said to be London's oldest surviving fish and chip shop, frying since 1871. It was badly hit by a bomb in the Second World War and rebuilt. A handy stop near the theatres.
Fish and chips on Marylebone Lane since 1914. The old enamelled fryer is still in the room, now holding menus. Family-run, and you can bring your own drinks.

sig: Cod and chips in beef dripping
ds: Opened in 1958 by two Italian brothers, and it still fries in beef dripping, the old way. Retro Formica tables, shared booths and no fuss.

a: 38 Muswell Hill Broadway, Muswell Hill, London N10 3RT
ds: A Muswell Hill chip shop for over fifty years, named after its first owner. A sit-down dining room or takeaway, with fish cooked fresh to order.

n: The Palm Court at The Ritz
a: The Ritz London, 150 Piccadilly, London W1J 9BR
ds: Afternoon tea at The Ritz, open since 1906, in a gilded room full of mirrors and chandeliers. It is a true special-occasion treat: book ahead, and gentlemen need a jacket and tie.

a: 77 Borough High Street, Southwark, London SE1 1NH
ds: London's last galleried coaching inn, rebuilt in the 1670s after a fire. It is owned by the National Trust and gets a mention in Dickens' Little Dorrit.
The Arment family has run this shop since 1914, now in its fourth generation. Pies are made with 100% beef steak, and the mash is just potatoes and salt.

n: Newens The Original Maids of Honour
ds: A family bakery and tea room at Kew since 1860, opposite Kew Gardens. Its warm Maids of Honour tart is said to go back to Henry VIII's court at Richmond.

a: 34-35 Maiden Lane, Covent Garden, London WC2E 7LB
ds: London's oldest restaurant, opened by Thomas Rule as an oyster bar in 1798. It is famous for British game, pies and puddings. Dickens, Chaplin and Graham Greene all ate here, and in 2026 the building was given to the National Trust.

sig: Roast rib of beef from the trolley
ds: Opened in 1828 as a chess club and cigar room, and famous for roast beef carved at your table from silver-domed trolleys. Jeremy King reopened it in March 2026 after five years shut.

a: 55 Jermyn Street, St James's, London SW1Y 6LX
ds: Began as an oyster stall on Haymarket in 1742 and has been on Jermyn Street since 1984. A smart, old-fashioned dining room for oysters, Dover sole and game in season.

a: 39 Queen Victoria Street, City of London EC4N 4SF
ds: A City fish restaurant at the same address since 1889. It opens for weekday lunch only and takes no bookings, so arrive early for fish pie, potted shrimps and a Black Velvet in a pewter tankard.

a: 26 St John Street, Smithfield, London EC1M 4AY
sig: Roast bone marrow and parsley salad
ds: Fergus Henderson's 'nose to tail' restaurant, opened in 1994 in an old smokehouse by Smithfield Market. It changed how Britain cooks. Order the roast bone marrow, then an Eccles cake with Lancashire cheese.
On Farringdon Road since 1869, and the windows still say 'Progressive working class caterer'. Sit in the original Grade II listed wooden booths for chops, steaks and its famous confit potatoes.
Rebuilt in 1667, the year after the Great Fire of London. Dark wood rooms, sawdust floors and an old Chop Room. Charles Dickens and Mark Twain drank here.
An inn has stood here since 1423, and the grill room, opened in 1952, is billed as London's oldest steakhouse. Come for dry-aged British steaks and its award-winning steak and kidney pie.
A Victorian Mayfair pub known for its award-winning homemade pies. Each one comes with greens, gravy and chips or mash. Sister pub to The Guinea Grill.

a: 33 Rose Street, Covent Garden, London WC2E 9EB
ds: A pub since at least 1772, down a small Covent Garden alley. It was once nicknamed the 'Bucket of Blood' for its bare-knuckle fights, and Charles Dickens drank here.
A pub since 1818 in a quiet Belgravia mews, once the officers' mess of the Foot Guards. The Duke of Wellington drank here. Said to be London's most haunted pub, it is known for its beef Wellington.
One of London's few pubs with a MICHELIN Star. The cooking is all about British game, much of the deer comes from the owners, and the venison Scotch egg is famous.

sig: Afternoon tea in the Imperial Room
ds: The very first Bettys, founded in Harrogate in 1919 by Swiss confectioner Frederick Belmont. Try a Yorkshire Fat Rascal, a big fruity scone, or have afternoon tea in the Imperial Room.

sig: Afternoon tea in the Belmont Room
ds: Opened in 1937, with rooms inspired by the Queen Mary ocean liner. In the Oak Room you can still see a mirror signed by Second World War airmen with a diamond pen.
Whitby's famous harbourside fish restaurant, in a merchant's house built in 1750. The late critic AA Gill called its fish and chips the best anywhere.
One of the oldest houses in Bath, and home of the Sally Lunn bun: a big, light bun served with sweet or savoury toppings. There is a small kitchen museum in the cellar.
A grand Georgian room from 1795 that Jane Austen wrote into her novels. Have afternoon tea to live music from the Pump Room Trio, and taste the warm spa water from the fountain.
A harbour-front chip shop in the fishing village of Anstruther, and a past winner of UK Fish and Chip Shop of the Year. Get a haddock supper and eat it by the boats.
Said to be Britain's last original temperance bar, serving alcohol-free drinks since the 1890s. The cordials are still brewed from herbs the old way. Try a sarsaparilla or dandelion and burdock.

a: 24a Bridge Street, Bradford on Avon BA15 1BY
ds: A cosy tea room in an old blacksmith's cottage, where staff serve in Victorian dress. The Tea Guild named it its Top Tea Place in 2009.
Cambridge's famous bakery, opened in 1920 by the Mason brothers, whose names are still on the shop front. People come for the sticky Chelsea buns, and the café does cream teas too.

a: Back Pool Fold, Chapel Walks, Manchester M2 1HN
ds: A Victorian chop house where the painter L.S. Lowry was a regular, and a life-size bronze of him now sits at the bar. Order the corned beef hash, the house dish.
Opened in 1867 by Thomas Studd, in a Grade II listed building with green-tiled arches. A Manchester classic for steak and kidney pudding and proper pies.
Claims to date from 1189 and to be England's oldest inn. The pub is built against the sandstone rock under Nottingham Castle, and its caves have been used as cellars for centuries.

n: Ye Olde Pork Pie Shoppe (Dickinson & Morris)
ds: Hand-raising Melton Mowbray pork pies on Nottingham Street since 1851, in a Grade II* listed building. Take one away or sit down in the Tasting Room.
A family pasty bakery on Hayle's East Quay since 1958, still run by the Philp family. The traditional Cornish pasty is the one to get.
Designed by Charles Rennie Mackintosh for Kate Cranston in 1903, and the last of his tearooms still in its original home. Come for afternoon tea and see the famous Salon de Luxe.
Edinburgh's original oyster bar, founded in 1826 and 200 years old in 2026. The 1861 building is famous for its Doulton tile pictures and stained-glass windows.
Frying fish in Brighton since 1926, and still run by the Bardsley family, now in its fourth generation. Try cod, huss or skate.

a: 6-8 Turk's Head Yard, off Briggate, Leeds LS1 6HB
ds: Leeds' oldest pub, first licensed as the Turk's Head in 1715. It hides down a narrow yard off Briggate, with a Victorian interior from 1895.
